title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 17: Serrano v. NLRC: Are Workers Entitled to Due Process Prior to Dismissal?
keywords: Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations
primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Serrano v. NLRC, promulgated January 27, 2000, in which the en banc Court, through Justice Mendoza, held that an employer's failure to give the required notice before a dismissal for an authorized cause is not a denial of due process but merely makes the termination 'ineffectual,' with back wages and no reinstatement, over the Dissents of Justice Puno and himself.

The background he supplies from his own earlier book: how the Court for ten years granted only an indemnity of P1,000 to P10,000 where just or authorized cause existed but due process was ignored, and how he had rankled at that cavalier treatment in MGG Marine Services, Better Buildings and Del Val and hoped the Court en banc would one day review the proper sanction.

The majority's three reasons, quoted at length -- that the Due Process Clause limits governmental and not private power, that notice under Article 283 is not an adversary proceeding but a chance to prepare for job loss and to let DOLE verify the economic cause, and that the requirement descends from the mesada of the 1882 Spanish Code of Commerce and the Termination Pay Law rather than from the Constitution -- plus the analogy to notarial rescission under Articles 1592 and 1191 of the Civil Code.

CJP's Dissent in three theses: the notice requirement rests on the Constitution and not merely the Labor Code; a dismissal without due process is illegal, so the remedy is reinstatement plus full back wages and a return to the status quo ante; and even the Labor Code, in Article 277(b), grants not only notice but 'ample opportunity to be heard,' with a single exception where due process would be impractical or futile.

Justice Puno's Dissent, reproduced at length, from the rule of audi alteram partem through his four numbered objections to his closing plea that 'to many employees, dismissal is their lethal injection.'

The separate positions of Justices Bellosillo ('disturbance compensation' of P10,000) and Vitug (unpaid wages, proportionate 13th month pay and P10,000 nominal damages), and CJP's Epilogue that the majority bought labor a larger monetary award at the price of a vital right, an issue he expects to be debated again.
sub_topics: The frame: in Serrano the Court answered in the negative the question whether workers are entitled to due process prior to dismissal, over the separate Dissents of Justice Puno and CJP himself.

The prior law: an employer had to prove both just or authorized cause and due process; dismissals without cause were illegal and drew reinstatement with back wages, but where cause was proven and due process ignored the employee got only an indemnity or nominal damages of P1,000 to P10,000.

CJP recalls Chapter VIII of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- 'Battles Over the Rights of Labor' -- where in MGG Marine Services, Better Buildings and Del Val he rankled at the Court's cavalier treatment of due process and hoped for an en banc review of the proper sanction.

The facts: Isetann Department Store phased out its entire Security Section as a cost-cutting measure and engaged an outside agency; Ruben Serrano, head of the Security Checkers Section, was terminated on October 11, 1991, the very day he received the notice.

The majority's holding: the lay-off was for redundancy, an authorized cause under Article 283, so separation pay of one month per year of service was due, management being entitled to determine what units are essential and whether work should be contracted out; the same-day notice denied him written notice, making the termination merely 'ineffectual' and compensable by back wages, not reinstatement.
Majority reason one: the Due Process Clause limits governmental power and does not apply to the exercise of private power, since only the State can take life, liberty or property.

Majority reason two: notice and hearing are required before organized society's powers are brought to bear; an Article 283 lay-off involves no charge and no adversary system, the 30-day notice serving to let the employee prepare for job loss and DOLE determine whether economic causes exist, while the time for notice and hearing under Article 282 is the trial stage before the NLRC.

Majority reason three and the history: the notice requirement traces to Article 302 of the Spanish Code of Commerce of 1882 and the mesada, through Article 2270 of the Civil Code, RA 1052 and RA 1787, to the 1981 implementing rules of BP 130 and the 1989 amendment of Article 277(b) by RA 6715 -- so the earlier regime cannot be said to have denied due process; and an employer cannot be an entirely impartial judge of his own cause.

The Justinian analogy: not all notice requirements are due process requirements, some being applications of the precept to act with justice and observe honesty and good faith, whose breach makes a party liable in damages rather than voiding his act -- as with notarial rescission under Articles 1592 and 1191 of the Civil Code.

CJP's Dissent opens with gratitude that the Court reexamined the ten-year doctrine and raised the award from a nominal indemnity to full back wages, before taking issue with the majority's legal basis.

His first thesis: the notice requirement finds basis not only in the Labor Code but, more importantly, in the due process clause of the Constitution, whose provisions are deemed written into every statute, contract and undertaking, employment being a property right.

His second thesis, supported by a long line of authority: where procedural due process is violated the proceedings are voided and the parties returned to the status quo ante -- Pepsi-Cola Bottling ('void and nonexistent'), People v. Bocar on courts being ousted of jurisdiction, Bacus v. Ople and Ang Tibay, PNB v. Apalisok, Fabella v. Court of Appeals reinstating schoolteachers, the bail cases, People v. Sevilleno on searching inquiry, People v. Parazo on a deaf-mute retardate denied a sign language expert, and a Comelec nickname resolution set aside for want of notice and hearing.

His third thesis: it is inaccurate to say the Labor Code grants notice alone, since Article 277(b) subjects termination to security of tenure and requires the employer to furnish a written statement of causes and to afford 'ample opportunity to be heard' -- a requirement he reads as applying to Articles 282, 283 and 284 alike.

He presses the internal contradiction: 'ineffectual' means having no legal force, so a dismissal with no legal effect should produce reinstatement plus full back wages, and limiting the consequence to back wages has no statutory basis.

The exception he preserves: where the employer can prove that compliance was impossible, impractical or gravely adverse -- as in Wenphil, where the employee was caught virtually in flagrante delicto after brandishing an ice scooper and shouting profanities -- the dismissal is not illegal, though a nominal sum may be given as a measure of compassion under Article 2221 of the Civil Code.

His critique of Wenphil's afterlife: it was applied perfunctorily to cases with no exigency at all, including Serrano's own same-day dismissal, so that 'Indemnity or damages has become an easy substitute for due process.'

His constitutional argument for private due process: traditional doctrine confined constitutional rights to claims against the State because only the State could violate them, but with liberalization, deregulation and privatization corporate behemoths and individuals may now abuse human rights, so the doctrine must be modified.

His moral close: due process begins with the employer, not the labor tribunals; the administration of justice begins with each of us in everyday dealings; and denial of due process is no less than a denial of justice itself.

Justice Puno's Dissent: audi alteram partem as the essence of procedural due process; the Wenphil-bred 'dismiss now, pay later' strategy; the pre-dismissal notice as the linchpin of an employee's defense; the greater need for scrutiny in Article 283 cases where the facts lie with the employer and DOLE is the equalizer; the Constitution's placement of labor rights in Article XIII; Kingsize Manufacturing and Batangas Laguna Tayabas Bus as proof of long-adopted private due process; the rejection of the vendor-vendee analogy because labor is 'neither a chattel nor a commodity'; and his plea that 'to many employees, dismissal is their lethal injection.'

The other opinions: Justice Bellosillo would sustain the termination as valid but irregular and give P10,000 as 'disturbance compensation'; Justice Vitug would award unpaid wages, proportionate 13th month pay and P10,000 in nominal damages.

The Epilogue: the majority gave labor a larger monetary award -- from indemnity to full back wages -- but deprived the working force of a vital right, a shift so fundamental that CJP predicts he and Justice Puno, and perhaps others, will see the issue debated again.

stances.claim: The worker's right to notice before dismissal is constitutional, not merely statutory -- the employee is entitled to due process not because of the Labor Code but because of the Constitution, whose provisions are deemed written into every statute and contract.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional relocation of the right, supported by the doctrine that employment is a property right

stances.claim: A dismissal effected without due process is illegal and void, so the employee must be returned to the status quo ante with reinstatement plus full back wages, not merely paid an indemnity or back wages.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument by accumulated precedent, marching through labor, administrative, criminal and election cases in which proceedings without notice were voided

stances.claim: The majority's label is self-contradictory: 'ineffectual' means having no legal force, and a dismissal with no legal force cannot at the same time produce the legal effect of a severed employment with back wages only.
stances.rhetorical_move: internal-contradiction attack on the majority's chosen term

stances.claim: The traditional rule confining constitutional rights to claims against the State must be modified, because with liberalization, deregulation and privatization corporate behemoths and individuals have become sources of abuse of human rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal updating argued from changed economic conditions

stances.claim: There is one exception: where compliance with due process was impossible, impractical or gravely adverse -- as where the employee is caught in flagrante delicto, the actual situation in Wenphil -- the dismissal is not illegal, though a nominal sum may be given as compassion.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrowing a precedent to its facts while preserving its legitimate core

stances.claim: Justice Puno held that the majority's ruling is a blow on the breadbasket of lowly employees and that the pre-dismissal notice is the linchpin of an employee's right against illegal dismissal.
stances.rhetorical_move: extended reproduction of a colleague's dissent as reinforcement

stances.claim: The majority bought labor a larger monetary award at the cost of a vital right, and the issue will be debated again.
stances.rhetorical_move: epilogue ledger of gain against loss, closing with a promise of continued dissent

notable_anecdotes: CJP traces the chapter to his own earlier book, recalling that in MGG Marine Services, Better Buildings and Del Val he 'rankled' at the Court's treatment of due process and ended Chapter VIII of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' hoping the en banc would one day review the proper sanction -- an opportunity that arrived with Serrano.

He notes that Serrano came only after 'more than a year of internal deliberations and debates' within the full Court, and that Ruben Serrano was dismissed on the very same day he received his notice of termination.
He opens his Dissent with a note of gratitude rather than attack, thanking the Court for reexamining the ten-year doctrine and for raising the award from a nominal indemnity to full back wages.

He revisits the facts of Wenphil to show why it was rightly decided on its own facts: the employee had slapped a co-worker's cap, stepped on his foot, brandished an ice scooper and shouted profane words at the assistant manager, caught virtually in flagrante delicto before many people.

He reproduces Justice Puno's closing plea about what a job means to an employee -- the schooling of children stopped, ejectment from leased premises, hunger, a life without a safety net -- and his line that 'to many employees, dismissal is their lethal injection.'
He ends the chapter by naming the future: the shift was so fundamental that 'Justice Puno and I -- and perhaps some other justices too -- will see to that' when the issue returns.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Serrano v. NLRC, promulgated January 27, 2000 after more than a year of internal debate, in which the en banc Court answered in the negative the question whether workers are entitled to due process before dismissal. Isetann Department Store had phased out its Security Section and terminated Ruben Serrano on the very day he received notice; Justice Mendoza, for the majority, held the lay-off a valid redundancy under Article 283, awarded separation pay, and characterized the defective notice as making the termination merely 'ineffectual,' compensable by full back wages rather than reinstatement. His reasons were that the Due Process Clause limits governmental and not private power, that an Article 283 notice serves to let the worker prepare and DOLE verify the economic cause rather than to answer a charge, that the requirement descends from the mesada of the 1882 Spanish Code of Commerce and the Termination Pay Law, and that failure to give it is like failing to make a notarial demand before rescinding a sale. Artemio V. Panganiban dissented, first thanking the Court for reexamining a ten-year doctrine under which he had long rankled at indemnities of P1,000 to P10,000, then arguing three theses: the notice requirement rests on the Constitution and not merely the Labor Code, since employment is a property right and constitutional provisions are written into every statute; a violation of procedural due process voids the proceeding and restores the status quo ante, as a long line of labor, administrative, criminal and election cases showed, so the remedy is reinstatement plus full back wages; and Article 277(b) itself grants ample opportunity to be heard. He preserved one exception, for cases like Wenphil where compliance was impractical or the employee was caught in flagrante delicto, and warned that indemnity had become an easy substitute for due process, letting the rich purchase a constitutional right granted to the poor. He reproduced Justice Puno's dissent at length and closed with his own creed -- due process begins with the employer, the administration of justice begins with each of us, and denial of due process is a denial of justice itself -- noting in the Epilogue that the majority had bought labor money at the price of a vital right.
